content: Tonic water, also known as Indian tonic water, is a carbonated soft drink that is flavored with quinine. The name tonic water originates from the medicinal properties of quinine, which imparts a slightly bitter taste to the beverage. Historically, quinine was added to tonic water as a prophylactic treatment for malaria, as the drink was initially intended for consumption in tropical regions of India and Africa where malaria is endemic. Originally, tonic water consisted solely of carbonated water and a high concentration of quinine. However, modern tonic water typically contains only a medically insignificant amount of quinine, and it is primarily consumed for its flavor rather than its therapeutic effects. As a result, contemporary tonic water is less bitter and is often sweetened. Additionally, some manufacturers produce diet versions of tonic water. In the United States, the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) regulates the quinine content in tonic water, limiting it to 83 parts per million (ppm), equivalent to 83 milligrams per liter by mass. This concentration is significantly lower—approximately one-half to one-quarter—than the amount used in therapeutic formulations of quinine. Tonic water is frequently used as a mixer in cocktails, particularly those made with gin, such as the classic gin and tonic. Variants of tonic water that include added lemon or lime flavoring are referred to as bitter lemon or bitter lime, respectively. These flavored soft drinks are more popular in Europe compared to the United States. One notable property of tonic water is its ability to fluoresce under ultraviolet (UV) light due to the presence of quinine. In fact, quinine is so sensitive to UV light that tonic water will even fluoresce in direct sunlight.
